claims.text: Fast thermal cycling kinetically traps noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles in a metastable single-phase solid-solution state.
A moderate thermal hold during heating enhances atomic diffusion.
Enhanced diffusion allows thermodynamic mixing tendencies to compete with elemental segregation.
A moderate thermal hold can alter the crystal structure and particle morphology at fixed composition.
The proposed intervention is an intermediate thermal hold during heating below the decomposition threshold.
The composition and synthesis atmosphere are held constant between the baseline and intervention.
The hold is restricted to a temperature range intended to permit diffusion without excessive coarsening or decomposition.
Atomic diffusion controls short-range ordering and the balance between segregation and mixing.
Rapid thermal cycling provides insufficient time for atoms to overcome local energy barriers.
The thermal hold permits atoms to diffuse more freely and can enable partial phase separation or elemental segregation.
Diffusion drives evolution from a kinetically trapped single phase toward an equilibrium state containing mixed phases and altered particle morphology.
Rapidly processed baseline nanoparticles are single-phase solid solutions with uniform morphology.
Compared with rapid processing, the thermal hold will produce phase separation or elemental segregation.
Compared with rapid processing, the thermal hold will change crystallographic peak patterns and particle faceting or size distributions.
Morphological shifts caused by the thermal hold may lower the thermal decomposition temperature.
The proposed mechanism applies to systems containing more than five noble-metal elements when processing remains below the decomposition threshold.
Specific elemental diffusivities and interactions determine the extent of phase separation and morphological change.
A lack of any statistically significant change in phase structure, elemental distribution, or morphology following the hold would falsify the proposed kinetic-control hypothesis.
